exam.title: CompTIA Network+ (V9)
exam.study_prerequisites: CompTIA recommends A+ knowledge plus 9–12 months of junior network administration or support experience. Practice end-to-end packet walks, IPv4 subnetting, media/transceiver selection, VLAN/STP/routing/NAT, wireless surveys, documentation/monitoring/recovery/services, segmentation/hardening, and evidence-led troubleshooting in an authorized lab.

review.notes: All five weighted V9 domains are mapped to an end-to-end packet-walk and evidence model, three scenarios, eight authorized labs and 42 original checks. The estimated-2027 statement is explicitly not an exact retirement date. All nine guide URLs are cataloged: seven reachable and O'Reilly plus Udemy automation-blocked; none missing or broken. No proprietary objective PDF, PBQ, course lab or recalled item is used.

findings.title: Full outline confirms modern-network scope beyond the summary
findings.evidence: Objective 1.8 includes SD-WAN, VXLAN, SASE/SSE, zero trust, IaC and IPv6 transitions; objective 5.1 explicitly includes methodology.
findings.recommendation: Map all 25 numbered objectives and teach these topics directly with original scenarios and references.
findings.resolution: Map all 25 numbered objectives and teach these topics directly with original scenarios and references.

findings.title: Route installation and forwarding were compressed into an ambiguous sequence
findings.evidence: Candidate installation uses route-source preference and protocol path selection; forwarding uses the longest matching installed prefix.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the distinction and execute a model for specific/default/host routes, missing routes and equal-prefix ambiguity.
findings.resolution: Rewrite the distinction and execute a model for specific/default/host routes, missing routes and equal-prefix ambiguity.

findings.title: Exhaustion was overgeneralized to existing renewals
findings.evidence: Lease renewal requests extension of an existing address and is distinct from new allocation.
findings.recommendation: Explain new-client versus existing-lease behavior, timers/rebinding/expiry, and qualified link-local evidence.
findings.resolution: Explain new-client versus existing-lease behavior, timers/rebinding/expiry, and qualified link-local evidence.

findings.title: PDF port label needed an operational security distinction
findings.evidence: PDF lists SMTPS 587; RFC 8314 distinguishes STARTTLS submission 587 and implicit TLS submission 465.
findings.recommendation: Keep the exam-listed port while teaching negotiation/identity checks and avoid claiming a port proves encryption.
findings.resolution: Keep the exam-listed port while teaching negotiation/identity checks and avoid claiming a port proves encryption.

findings.title: DNS response and transport security needed separate evidence
findings.evidence: DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and denial but does not provide confidentiality; encrypted transport has a different scope.
findings.recommendation: Add record/response/privacy tables and a real isolated DNS exercise; do not claim DNSSEC/TLS/cache execution.
findings.resolution: Add record/response/privacy tables and a real isolated DNS exercise; do not claim DNSSEC/TLS/cache execution.

findings.title: Small successful probes do not establish a working path MTU
findings.evidence: IPv6 PMTU depends on Packet Too Big feedback; blocked feedback can cause larger transfers to stall.
findings.recommendation: Add qualified VXLAN overhead calculations and distinguish IPv6 source fragmentation from router behavior; no path reconfiguration executed.
findings.resolution: Add qualified VXLAN overhead calculations and distinguish IPv6 source fragmentation from router behavior; no path reconfiguration executed.

72 harness checks and two public examples ran locally; 24 total DNS exchanges bound only to 127.0.0.1, with no upstream queries. Listeners stopped and sockets released.
Subnet, forwarding, MTU, PoE and transfer-rate cases are calculations/models, not configured device behavior.

The tiny DNS zone supports only selected demonstration behavior and is not a production authoritative/recursive implementation.
All eight complete network labs remain proposed.
Two OReilly pages and Udemy blocked automated rechecking; paid interiors and current book runtimes/page counts were not reverified.
Retirement remains an estimate of 2027, not an exact date.

        NOTE: The meaning of this service type, though called just "http", actually
        denotes something more precise than just "any data transported using HTTP".
        The DNS-SD service type "http" should only be used to advertise content that:
        * is served over HTTP,
        * can be displayed by "typical" web browser client software, and
        * is intented primarily to be viewed by a human user.
        Of course, the definition of "typical web browser" is subjective, and may
        change over time, but for practical purposes the DNS-SD service type "http"
        can be understood as meaning "human-readable HTML content served over HTTP".
        In some cases other widely-supported content types may also be appropriate,
        such as plain text over HTTP, or JPEG image over HTTP.
        Content types not intented primarily for viewing by a human user, or not
        widely-supported in web browsing clients, should not be advertised as
        DNS-SD service type "http", even if they do happen to be transported over HTTP.
        Such types should be advertised as their own logical service type with their
        own DNS-SD service type, for example, XUL (XML User Interface Language)
        transported over HTTP is advertised explicitly as DNS-SD service type "xul-http".
